methods.name: Prompt2Effect
methods.full_name: Prompt2Effect: weight-driven hypernetwork for SVD-canonicalized LoRA prediction
methods.paper_title: Prompt2Effect: Training-Free Image-to-Video Model Specialization via LoRA Generation
methods.formula_latex: X_W^{l}=\big[\,W_0^{l}P_B^{l}\,;\,(W_0^{l})^{\top}P_A^{l}\,\big]\in\mathbb{R}^{(d_{out}+d_{in})\times d_h},\ \ Q_W^{l}=\mathrm{CrossAttn}(Q_{\text{learned}},X_W^{l},X_W^{l})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_h};\ \ X_{\mathcal{E}}=H_{\mathcal{E}}\big(\{Q_W^{l}+e_l+e_M^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L},\,E_{\text{text}}(c_{\text{eff}})\big);\ \ X_{\mathcal{D}}^{l}=\mathrm{CrossAttn}(X_W^{l},X_{\mathcal{E}}^{l},X_{\mathcal{E}}^{l});\ \ \hat B^{l}=\mathrm{Head}_B\big(X_{\mathcal{D}}^{l}[:d_{out}]\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r},\ \ \hat A^{l}=\mathrm{Head}_A\big(X_{\mathcal{D}}^{l}[d_{out}:]\big)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}};\ \ h=(W_0^{l}+\hat B^{l}\hat A^{l})\,x;\ \ \text{targets: }\Delta W_{\star}^{l}=U^{l}S^{l}(V^{l})^{\top}\Rightarrow B^{\star,l}=U^{l}(S^{l})^{1/2},\ A^{\star,l}=(S^{l})^{1/2}(V^{l})^{\top};\ \ \min_{\phi}\ \frac{1}{2L}\sum_{l=1}^{L}\Big(\frac{\|\hat A^{l}-A^{\star,l}\|_F^2}{\|A^{\star,l}\|_F^2+\epsilon}+\frac{\|\hat B^{l}-B^{\star,l}\|_F^2}{\|B^{\star,l}\|_F^2+\epsilon}\Big);\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0,\ E_{\text{text}};\ \text{trained once: hypernetwork } \phi=(H_{\mathcal{E}},H_{\mathcal{D}},P_A,P_B,Q_{\text{learned}},e);\ \text{nothing trained per effect}
methods.trainable_params: |\phi|\approx 1.3\text{B (one hypernetwork, trained once by regression on 70 per-effect LoRAs; }\approx12\%\text{ of the 11B base)};\ \text{per new effect: } 0\ \text{trained, generated adapter } r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{per adapted matrix } (r=128)
methods.locus: LoRA target layers (a selected set of L linear layers) of a DiT image-to-video diffusion model: Snap's proprietary 11B I2V model, with the findings reproduced on Wan2.1-I2V-14B
methods.structure: Amortised LoRA generation: one 1.3B Transformer hypernetwork maps \((c_{\text{eff}},\{W_0^{l}\}_{l=1}^{L})\) to all layer-wise rank-\(r\) factor pairs \((\hat B^{l},\hat A^{l})\) in a single forward pass. The frozen base matrix is tokenised CUR-style into its \(d_{out}\) rows and \(d_{in}\) columns at full rank (truncating \(W_0\) to its top singular directions hurt in ablation). These tokens are compressed by learned-query cross-attention to \(n=256\) latents and mixed with the prompt by cross-attention. They are then decompressed by cross-attention that uses the original row and column tokens as queries, so the rows of \(\hat B^{l}\) and the columns of \(\hat A^{l}\) are indexed by the same coordinates as \(W_0^{l}\). The regression targets are SVD-canonicalised: the gauge orbit \(\{(BR,R^{-1}A):R\in GL(r)\}\) of each trained LoRA is replaced by its balanced representative \((US^{1/2},S^{1/2}V^{\top})\), which is unique up to joint sign flips of paired singular vectors (and rotations inside repeated singular values). The deployed object is an ordinary additive low-rank delta \(\Delta W^{l}=\hat B^{l}\hat A^{l}\).
methods.mergeable_reason: Each generated update \(\Delta W^{l}=\hat B^{l}\hat A^{l}\) is a plain low-rank additive delta that can be folded into \(W_0^{l}\) for a given effect. Generated deltas also blend linearly in weight space: the paper composes two effects as \(\Delta W=0.5\,\Delta W_A+0.5\,\Delta W_B\). The hypernetwork is needed only to produce new effects.
methods.identity_at_init: Not identity by design, since a non-zero \(\Delta W^{l}\) is the output. Dropping the generated LoRA recovers the frozen base. When the prediction is used to initialise LoRA fine-tuning, training starts from \(B_0=\hat B,\ A_0=\hat A\) instead of \(B_0=0\).
methods.key_idea: A LoRA delta is defined relative to \(W_0\), so the generator is conditioned on the full-rank base weights (tokenised by rows and columns) as well as the effect prompt. The factorisation gauge \((B,A)\sim(BR,R^{-1}A)\) is removed by regressing SVD-canonical factors \((US^{1/2},S^{1/2}V^{\top})\). Together these two choices make one-pass LoRA synthesis stable at video-DiT scale, where a HyperDreamBooth-style generator fails to train.
methods.results_note: On Snap's 11B image-to-video model, the zero-shot predicted LoRAs come close to per-effect trained LoRAs while replacing about 56 GPU-hours of training with 3.3 s of hypernetwork inference. Used as an initialisation, 100 fine-tuning steps reach an overall VLM score of 56.33 on out-of-distribution effects, versus 56.70 for a 1,000-step LoRA trained from scratch.

relations.note: Cited prompt-to-LoRA hypernetwork. Prompt2Effect is likewise trained by reconstructing a library of LoRAs, but conditions on the base weights as well as the text and regresses SVD-canonicalised factors.
A HyperDreamBooth-style hypernetwork is the main learned baseline. Scaled to video LoRAs it trains unstably and gives near-zero VLM scores.
Cited prompt-to-weights generator for LLMs. Prompt2Effect targets video DiTs and adds base-weight conditioning.

Same amortised LoRA-generation line (not cited). D2L conditions on the frozen model's activations over a document and trains by context distillation. Prompt2Effect conditions on the frozen weights and an effect prompt and trains by regression on a LoRA library.

Two treatments of the same GL(r) symmetry of LoRA factors (not cited). Prompt2Effect picks a canonical SVD representative of each orbit; Learning on LoRAs builds GL-equivariant networks that act on whole orbits.

methods.name: GiVA
methods.paper_title: GiVA: Gradient-Informed Bases for Vector-Based Adaptation
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+\Gamma B\,\Lambda A\,x,\quad \Gamma=\mathrm{diag}(\gamma),\ \gamma\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}},\ \ \Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda),\ \lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{r};\ \ G=\nabla_W\mathcal{L}(W_0)\ \text{(full fine-tuning gradient on one batch)},\ G\approx U\Sigma V^{\top}\ \text{(low-rank SVD)};\ \ A=V_r^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}},\ \ B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}\ \text{with } B^{\top}B=I_r\ \ (\text{TopSV-B: } U_{[:,1:r]},\ \text{SecSV-B: } U_{[:,r+1:2r]},\ \text{Rand-B: QR of a Gaussian});\ \ \gamma_0=0,\ \lambda_0=\mathbf{1};\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0,\ A,\ B\ \text{(per layer)};\ \text{trained: } \gamma,\ \lambda
methods.trainable_params: d_{out}+r\ \text{per adapted matrix (plus frozen per-layer bases, } r(d_{in}+d_{out})\text{, stored once per task)}
methods.locus: any linear layer; paper: attention and MLP projections of RoBERTa (GLUE), Qwen2-0.5B, Phi-3-3.8B and OLMo-2-7B (commonsense, math, code, instruction tuning), DINOv2-ViT-B/14 and CLIP-ViT-L/14 (image classification)
methods.structure: This is VeRA-type vector adaptation \(\Delta W=\Gamma B\Lambda A\): two trainable diagonals around a frozen rank-\(r\) pair. Unlike VeRA, the frozen pair is per-layer and task-informed rather than shared and random. \(A\) spans the top-\(r\) right singular subspace of the one-batch full fine-tuning gradient \(G\), and \(B\) is any matrix with orthonormal columns. Theorem 1 shows this choice minimises \(\|GA^{\top}B^{\top}BA-G\|_F\): it makes \(GA^{\top}B^{\top}BA=GV_rV_r^{\top}\) the best rank-\(r\) approximation of \(G\) (Eckart-Young). The objective comes from a first-order expansion at \(\Gamma_0=0,\Lambda_0=I\) that writes \(\nabla_\Gamma\mathcal{L}\) as the full matrix \(GA^{\top}B^{\top}\). For the diagonal \(\Gamma\) actually trained, only the diagonal of that matrix is used, so the matching is exact only for this relaxation. After training, the row space of \(\Delta W\) lies in the fixed subspace \(\mathrm{span}(V_r)\) and its column space in \(\Gamma\,\mathrm{span}(B)\). The trainable freedom is an \(r\)-vector rescaling of the frozen directions plus a \(d_{out}\)-vector rescaling of output coordinates.
methods.mergeable_reason: After training, \(\Delta W=\Gamma B\Lambda A\) is a fixed matrix of rank at most \(r\) that folds into \(W_0\), as with VeRA.
methods.identity_at_init: Exact: \(\gamma_0=0\) gives \(\Delta W_0=0\). Because \(\Gamma_0=0\), the gradient with respect to \(\lambda\) is zero at the first step, so only \(\gamma\) moves initially.
methods.key_idea: Vector-based adapters such as VeRA need very high rank (e.g. \(r=1024\)) because their frozen bases are random and carry no task information. GiVA sets the bases to the dominant right singular vectors of the first-step full fine-tuning gradient, with \(B\) orthonormal. The same \(d_{out}+r\) trainable scalars then suffice at about one-eighth of the rank, which brings training time close to LoRA's.
methods.results_note: On GLUE with RoBERTa-base, GiVA at \(r=8\) (0.08M trainable parameters, Rand-B) averages 83.8, versus 83.6 for VeRA at \(r=1024\) (0.16M) and 83.3 for LoRA at \(r=4\). Fine-tuning OLMo-2-7B on MetaMathQA takes 2h57m, versus 2h54m for LoRA and 3h26m for VeRA.

relations.note: Same \(\Gamma B\Lambda A\) parameterisation and scaling-vector initialisation. The frozen shared random bases are replaced by per-layer gradient-SVD bases.

Borrows the first-step full-gradient SVD initialisation. LoRA-GA then trains A and B, whereas GiVA freezes them and trains only the two scaling vectors. The SecSV-B variant mirrors LoRA-GA's use of singular vectors r+1..2r.
The TopSV-B variant uses the top left singular vectors of the gradient, as LoRA-One does for LoRA.
Also freezes gradient-initialised low-rank bases and trains a tiny core (r^2 entries); GiVA trains d_out + r diagonal entries instead.
Vector-based baseline with frozen random bases and full-rank updates.
Another VeRA derivative. It keeps random bases and makes the bottleneck stochastic instead of task-informed.

methods.name: AP (Activation Prompt)
methods.full_name: Activation Prompt: universal additive perturbation of one intermediate activation map
methods.paper_title: Visual prompting reimagined: The power of the Activation Prompts
methods.formula_latex: z^{(k)}=f_{\theta^{(k)}}\big(z^{(k-1)}\big),\ z^{(0)}=x;\quad z^{(l)}\ \leftarrow\ z^{(l)}+\delta^{(l)}\ \text{at a single chosen layer } l,\ \ \delta^{(l)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D'\times P'}\ \ (\text{channels}\times\text{spatial positions for CNNs};\ d\times\text{tokens for ViTs});\quad \min_{\delta^{(l)},\,W_{head}}\ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}}\ell\big(f_{\theta}(x,\delta^{(l)});y\big);\ \ l=0\ \text{recovers additive input-level VP};\ \ \text{frozen: backbone } \theta;\ \text{trained: } \delta^{(l)}\ \text{and the linear head}
methods.trainable_params: D'P'=|z^{(l)}|\ \text{(one activation-sized tensor, e.g. } d\times\text{tokens at a ViT block input)}+|W_{head}|;\ \text{reported totals including the head: } 0.12\text{M (ResNet-101)},\ 0.16\text{M (ViT-L/16)}
methods.locus: a single intermediate activation map: by default the input of the third-to-last residual block of ResNet-101 (CNNs prefer deep layers) and the input of the third Transformer block of ViT-L/16 (ViTs prefer shallow layers); also tested on CLIP and Swin
methods.structure: An input-independent additive offset \(z^{(l)}\mapsto z^{(l)}+\delta^{(l)}\) on the full activation tensor of one layer. Each channel and each position gets its own value, so this is a constant bias map rather than a per-channel bias. Input-level VP is the case \(l=0\). Proposition 1: if \(\delta^{(l)}\) is the same at every position and the normaliser has unit effective scale (\(\gamma_d/\sigma=1\)), AP coincides with shift-only BatchNorm/LayerNorm tuning at that layer. For CNNs the correspondence is \(\beta_d=w_d^{(l)}\delta_*+\mu_d\); for ViTs it is \(\beta=\delta_*\) when \(\mu=0\). AP is therefore a position-resolved generalisation of a single-layer shift. Unlike VPT, it adds no tokens and touches one layer. Backpropagation only has to reach layer \(l\), so a deep \(l\) in a CNN cuts training memory and time.
methods.mergeable_reason: \(\delta^{(l)}\) is a fixed tensor added to the activations, so inference costs one addition and no extra matmuls. It can be absorbed into the bias or normalisation shift of the adjacent layer only when it is the same at every position (Proposition 1). A position-specific \(\delta^{(l)}\) must be kept as a stored constant bias map.
methods.identity_at_init: Exact when \(\delta^{(l)}=0\), because the frozen network is then unchanged. The paper does not state how \(\delta^{(l)}\) is initialised. The linear head is trained as in linear probing.
methods.key_idea: Moving the universal additive prompt from pixels to one intermediate activation turns visual prompting into a single-layer activation shift that is provably related to normalisation tuning. The best layer depends on the architecture (deep for CNNs, shallow for ViTs), which the authors tie to where global features live. A two-layer-ViT theorem shows that shallow AP needs \(N=\Theta(P)\) samples, while deep AP needs \(N=\Theta(P^{2}\log P)\), where \(P\) is the number of tokens.
methods.results_note: Across 19 FGVC, VTAB and other datasets, AP beats input-level VP on every dataset for both ResNet-101 and ViT-L/16, with average gains of about 4% and 1.5%. On ResNet-101 it also nearly halves training memory relative to VP (6.3 GB vs 12.2 GB).

relations.note: Additive input-level VP is AP at layer l = 0; the paper uses AP to explain why VP lags.
With a position-uniform offset and unit effective scale, AP reduces to shift-only LayerNorm/BatchNorm tuning at one layer (Proposition 1).
VPT prepends tokens at the input or at every layer. AP adds a bias map at one chosen layer and matches or beats VPT-deep on ViT-L/16 at lower cost.

Both edit activations without touching weights. RED applies a per-channel scale and bias, shared across positions, at every FFN output; AP is bias-only but position-specific and confined to one layer.
LoFiT adds learned offset vectors to selected attention-head outputs; AP adds an offset to an entire activation map of one layer.
SSF's scale-and-shift feature modulation in every layer is a compared PEFT baseline.

methods.name: Stable-LoRA
methods.full_name: Stable-LoRA: early-step weight shrinkage of the LoRA down-projection
methods.paper_title: Stable-LoRA: Stabilizing Feature Learning of Low-Rank Adaptation
methods.formula_latex: h=W_0x+s\,BAx,\quad B_0=0,\ \ A_0\ \text{entries sampled from } [-1/d_{in},\,1/d_{in}];\ \ \text{while not stable: if } \|A_t\|_F/d_{in}>\|B_t\|_F/d_{out}\ \text{then } A_t\leftarrow(1-\lambda)A_t\ \text{else set stable};\ \ A_{t+1}=A_t-\eta g_A^t-\eta wA_t,\ \ B_{t+1}=B_t-\eta g_B^t-\eta wB_t\ \ (g=\text{AdamW-processed gradients},\ w=\text{weight decay});\ \ \lambda\in[5\times10^{-4},\,5\times10^{-3}];\ \ \text{frozen: } W_0;\ \text{trained: } A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}},\ B\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r}
methods.trainable_params: r(d_{in}+d_{out})\ \text{(identical to LoRA; the shrinkage is in place, so no extra memory)}
methods.locus: any LoRA-adapted linear layer; paper default q_proj and v_proj (r = 8) of Qwen2-0.5B/1.5B and LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, with ablations on other target modules
methods.structure: The parameterisation is plain LoRA, \(\Delta W=sBA\); only the optimisation trajectory changes. During the first few steps, an in-place multiplicative decay \(A\leftarrow(1-\lambda)A\), independent of the learning rate, is applied to the down-projection only. It stops once the balance condition \(\|A\|_F/d_{in}\le\|B\|_F/d_{out}\) holds, after which training is ordinary AdamW. Because only \(A\) is shrunk, each shrink step rescales the current update \(\Delta W\) by \((1-\lambda)\). This differs from a gauge move \((A,B)\mapsto(cA,B/c)\), which would leave \(\Delta W\) unchanged. After \(N\) shrink steps the initialisation enters \(A_N\) only through \((1-\lambda)^{N}A_0\).
methods.mergeable_reason: The trained adapter is a standard \(sBA\) and merges like LoRA; the procedure changes only how \(A\) and \(B\) are reached.
methods.identity_at_init: Exact: \(B_0=0\) gives \(\Delta W_0=0\). Shrinking \(A\) while \(B=0\) leaves the function unchanged; later shrink steps scale \(\Delta W\) by \((1-\lambda)\).
methods.key_idea: The paper writes \(v=\Theta(n^{\gamma[v]})\) for scaling in the width \(n\) and assumes Adam-normalised gradients with \(\gamma[g_A^tZ]=1\). Under these conditions, LoRA is self-stabilised, meaning feature updates \(\Delta Y_t=\Theta(1)\) for all \(t\), when \(\gamma[s]+2\gamma[\eta]+1=0\), \(\gamma[A_0Z]\le\gamma[\eta]+1\) and \(\gamma[B_0]\le\gamma[\eta]\) (Theorem 3.1). The usual non-zero \(A_0\) violates the \(A_0\) condition at practical learning rates, and the violation persists through training. Stable-LoRA therefore keeps \(A_0\)'s early benefit (escaping the saddle at zero) but decays it geometrically until the balance condition holds.
methods.results_note: On Qwen2 (0.5B, 1.5B) and LLaMA-3.2 (1B, 3B) multiple-choice QA, Stable-LoRA consistently outperforms AdamW-LoRA, LoRA+, Riemannian preconditioning and LoRA-RITE, by up to 4% accuracy, at 0.6% extra training time and no extra memory. It also beats AdamW-LoRA on MetaMathQA-to-GSM8K chain-of-thought training.

relations.note: Same parameterisation; only the training procedure changes.
LoRA+ restores width-stable feature learning with eta_B > eta_A. Stable-LoRA keeps one learning rate and decays A early. LoRA+ is a baseline.
Alternative route to stable LoRA feature learning (r x r preconditioners), used as a baseline. It costs +8.3% training time versus +0.6% for Stable-LoRA in their timing.
Transformation-invariant LoRA optimiser, used as a baseline. It costs +46% training time versus +0.6% for Stable-LoRA.

Keeps the init B_0 = 0, A_0 != 0 that Hayou et al. favour. Stable-LoRA shows that this non-zero A_0 breaks width-stability unless the learning rate is large enough, and removes its long-term effect by shrinkage.

methods.name: MDPD
methods.full_name: Masked Dual Path Distillation with fading side networks
methods.paper_title: Memory-Efficient Transfer Learning with Fading Side Networks via Masked Dual Path Distillation
methods.formula_latex: b^{1:L}=\Phi_{1:L}\big(x;\theta_0,\{\gamma_l,\beta_l\}_{l=1}^{L}\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D_B},\ \ s^{l}=\Theta_l\big(s^{l-1},\mathrm{fuse}(b^{l},b^{L})\big)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D_S},\ D_S<D_B;\ \ Y^{B}=W_B\,\mathrm{GAP}(b^{L}),\ Y^{S}=W_S\,\mathrm{GAP}(s^{L});\ \ \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{task}(Y^{S},y)+\lambda_{log}\sum_i\big(Y^{S}_i-\phi(Y^{B})_i\big)^2+\lambda_{sha}\sum_{l\in\text{shallow}}\big\|b^{l}-s^{l}M_{down}M_{up}\big\|_F^2+\lambda_{deep}\sum_{l\in\text{deep}}\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_i\big\|b^{l}_i-\mathcal{G}(\bar s^{l})_i\big\|^2,\ \ \bar s^{l}_i=\begin{cases}f_{mask}, & m_i=1\ (\text{mask ratio }\lambda)\\ s^{l}_i, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases};\ \ \text{frozen: backbone weights } \theta_0;\ \text{trained: per-block LayerNorm } (\gamma_l,\beta_l),\ W_B,\ \text{side network } \Theta,\ W_S,\ \text{bottlenecks } M_{down},M_{up},\ \mathcal{G},\ f_{mask};\ \ \text{inference: } \hat y=W_B\,\mathrm{GAP}\big(\Phi_{1:L}(x;\theta_0,\{\gamma_l,\beta_l\})\big)\ \text{(side network discarded)}
methods.locus: training: a thin side network (widths divided by a reduction factor, initialised from pretrained weights) fed by the backbone's per-layer features, plus distillation bottlenecks and a generator; deployed: the LayerNorm affine parameters of every backbone block and a new task head (ViT-B on VTAB-1K, T5-base/large on GLUE, VSE-infinity, CLIP4Clip, CLIP-ViL and MDETR for vision-language tasks)
methods.structure: A training-only ladder side network serves as scaffolding and is discarded at inference. Two distillation paths couple it to the frozen backbone. In the feature path (backbone to side), each side layer is regressed onto the backbone's features: directly through a bottleneck \(\phi(s)=sM_{down}M_{up}\) in shallow layers, and in deep layers by regenerating the teacher features from masked student tokens with a small convolutional generator \(\mathcal{G}\). In the logit path (side to backbone), the task-trained side head teaches a new backbone head \(W_B\). The only trainable state left in the backbone is the per-block LayerNorm \((\gamma,\beta)\) plus \(W_B\), so the deployed model is exactly a LayerNorm-tuned backbone. The side network acts as an auxiliary teacher whose task knowledge is distilled into that selective subset.
methods.mergeable_reason: The deployed model changes only LayerNorm affine parameters and adds a head, with no extra modules or tokens. The new \((\gamma,\beta)\) simply replace the pretrained ones and can be folded into the adjacent linear layer. The side network, the bottlenecks \(\phi\) and the generator \(\mathcal{G}\) are discarded.
methods.identity_at_init: Backbone features are unchanged at initialisation: \((\gamma_l,\beta_l)\) start at their pretrained values, and the side network does not feed back into the backbone. The task heads \(W_B,W_S\) are new, so the output layer is not identity-initialised.
methods.key_idea: Memory-efficient side-tuning keeps its side network at inference and pays for it in latency. MDPD instead uses the side network as a training-time teacher, mutually distilled with the frozen backbone. Its task knowledge ends up in the backbone's LayerNorm \((\gamma,\beta)\) and head, so it can be dropped at deployment.
methods.results_note: On vision-language tasks MDPD improves accuracy over UniPT and SHERL at almost the same training memory and cuts SHERL's inference time by at least 25.2%. On VTAB-1K with ViT-B it reports the best average among the compared PETL and METL methods.

relations.note: Uses an LST-style side network with ladder inputs from the backbone layers and LST's T5 layer-dropping, and is compared against LST. Unlike LST, the side network is dropped at inference.
The deployed model is a LayerNorm-tuned backbone plus head. MDPD learns those LayerNorm parameters through distillation from a side network instead of the task loss alone.
Res-Tuning (whose Bypass variant is also memory-efficient) is a compared baseline.

notes: All five requested methods exist and none duplicates a catalogued id (checked against existing_index.json, raw/, verified/ and addenda/). Every method was read from its arXiv HTML method section; the arXiv export API and Semantic Scholar both returned HTTP 429, so metadata came from arxiv.org/abs pages and the OpenReview search API. Venues verified: Stable-LoRA is an ICLR 2026 poster (OpenReview xSa19DAieH). GiVA is an AISTATS 2026 spotlight (80lrQEKKJg). AP is an AISTATS 2026 poster (7onqhBs7NV). MDPD is in CVF open access for CVPR 2026. Prompt2Effect is ECCV 2026 per its arXiv comment and project page. Year follows the first public version: Stable-LoRA = 2025, because the ICLR 2026 submission was public on OpenReview from 2025-10-08 and arXiv v1 came on 2026-03-05. AP = 2023, because the same paper was a public ICLR 2024 submission (OpenReview 0b328CMwn1, open 2023-10-13) before a withdrawn ICLR 2025 version, the CPAL 2025 spotlight track, a TMLR rejection and finally AISTATS 2026; arXiv v1 is 2026-04-07. Prompt2Effect: the original Snap code is not public. The project page links an independent reproduction on Wan2.1 (https://github.com/LukeLIN-web/Prompt2Effect), so code_url is left empty. GiVA: the paper's derivation treats the gradient with respect to the diagonal output scaling as a full matrix, so the first-step-matching optimality (Theorem 1) holds for that relaxation; this is recorded in the structure field. OSoRA, a GiVA baseline that takes its bases from the SVD of W_0, is not in the catalogue. MDPD: the deployed model is a LayerNorm-tuned backbone plus head. The paper says LayerNorm parameters in every backbone block are updated, but does not explain how they get gradients without backpropagating through the backbone, which would cut against the memory claims. Confidence is therefore medium. None of the five is in Hugging Face PEFT (tuners directory and releases up to v0.21.2 checked). No standalone theory papers were added; the stability theorem (Stable-LoRA) and the sample-complexity theorem (AP) are recorded inside the method entries.
